structure.title: Chapters 1–3 · At the table, in bed, on a screen
structure.text: Stupple opens the fridge before he opens the philosophical argument. Food, sleep and videos are three places where an adult can impose a decision almost effortlessly. His descriptions of his own children give those decisions a second side. The child who wants the screen back may have unfinished business with an octopus.

structure.title: Chapters 4–5 · What obedience leaves unresolved
structure.text: Once a child obeys, a disagreement becomes harder to see. Stupple builds his case against rules around what the parent then misses, including objections that might have changed the parent's mind. His alternative requires the adult to help invent an arrangement that everyone involved can accept.

structure.title: Chapters 6–9 · The child running into the street
structure.text: The obvious objection gets its turn. Stupple would pull a child away from a car, just as he would pull an adult away. The harder cases take longer than a rescue. Siblings can want incompatible things, and a family that has relied on rules for years must work out how to change its habits together.

structure.title: Chapters 10–11 · Why a parent might welcome an objection
structure.text: The philosophy arrives after its consequences have had time to bother the reader. If people learn by proposing ideas and finding mistakes in them, a child's objection can help a family discover an error. Stupple asks how differently adults might have grown up if someone had treated their objections that way.

people.name: Aaron Stupple
people.role: Father of five and the adult in the examples
people.text: The children can refuse a meal or protest at bedtime. Stupple can buy different food, rearrange an evening, or simply insist. His accounts are most revealing when he describes what he did with a power the other person in the room did not possess.

people.name: Taking Children Seriously
people.text: An adult who takes a child's preference seriously still has preferences, responsibilities and ideas of her own. The difficult part is what follows when they clash. Much of the book describes the work adults take on when making a child comply is no longer their usual way of ending a dispute.

context.title: A household experiment and a general claim
context.text: A story about one child's appetite can reveal an assumption his father had overlooked. Stupple also makes broad claims about what enforcing rules does to families. These two kinds of evidence carry different weight, even when they appear on the same page.

passages.quote: Eating may be the most personal human experience.

notice.text: Listen to the son's account of his screen time.
notice.why: Hours on a tablet look much the same on a clock. In the boy's conversation those hours have different subjects, from sea mammals to Godzilla. Knowing what occupied him changes the question his father thinks he needs to answer.

passages.quote: octopi and squids, sea mammals, and Godzilla.

notice.text: Keep track of who supplies the next idea.
notice.why: Ending an argument by withdrawing a rule can leave both people exactly where they started. The practical examples turn on the next move, when one of them discovers a different meal, activity or arrangement that the other can welcome.

opening: A child wants to keep playing; a parent says it is bedtime. The parent can end the dispute by exercising authority, but Aaron Stupple asks what has actually been resolved. Drawing on life with his five children, he argues for abandoning rules in favour of finding solutions that take the child's reasons seriously. His proposal reaches into food, screens, and the daily negotiations of family life, challenging the assumption that preparing someone for independence requires years of making their choices for them.
